 Netflix ’s anime viewership is struggling to hold a dominant position in the country where the medium originated. As per a reader survey published on Nov. 5, 2026, by the Japanese website, Anime! Anime! , only around 15 percent of respondents most of the time watch anime through subscription platforms, while 70% watch live broadcast television; the latter wins this game by a huge margin.
 The survey was called Anime! Anime! “Oshi-katsu”, which also covers manga and games, and the study was not specific to Netflix. The exact sample size of the readers was not revealed; even so, one can assume the readership of one of the biggest media outlets in Japan. Despite this, the poll percentage clearly shows how much ground streaming services still have to cover to influence the deep culture.
 Broadcast Still Rules Anime Viewing in Japan
 × Remove Ads
 Netflix’s catalogue of anime | Credits: Netflix 
 The outlet asked its participants whether they watch anime live as it telecasts on television. About 55% of them said that they occasionally watch episodes at the premiere time, while about 20% of the participants came out as regular real-time viewers. This means more than 70% of participants were in this section.
 Recording a television broadcast is also popular in Japan, with about 45% of participants taping their favourite anime to watch later or rewatch. By comparison, only about 15% of the respondents watch anime through subscription platforms. The outlet also gave one of the most surprising statistics: Nearly half of the respondents did not have current subscriptions.
 × Remove Ads
 This poll suggests that live telecast is still a vital part of anime viewing culture in Japan. While streaming is more flexible and gives its viewers more options through its extensive collection, many of them like to follow their favourite shows as per their original broadcast times.
 This also highlights the continued relevance of the traditional weekly release model in a market where streaming platforms have become increasingly prominent.
 Netflix Trails Amazon Prime Video in Subscription Viewing.

 The polls also surveyed which platform service the participants used most to watch anime. Amazon Prime Video was victorious, the most frequently mentioned service. About half of users cited Amazon Prime Video, followed by Netflix at around 30%, while U-NEXT and Hulu trailed at around 10% each. 
 The polls show a notable hurdle for Netflix, which has repeatedly prioritized anime as an important part of its global content strategy. Although the platform has many popular and exclusive anime projects on its table and has expanded its anime catalogue, the Japanese telecasting culture doesn’t let subscription platforms dominate in their country.
 However, these figures from the outlet represent the preferences of the people who participated in the Oshi-katsu survey, and those who use these services, rather than the overall market share of each of the services. The outlet never established that Netflix’s anime collection is not doing great, and a broader poll could look totally different.
 As per the comprehensive market data from Media Partners Asia , anime makes up 28 % of tracked premium video-on-demand viewing hours in Japan in the first half of 2026. While Prime Video leads domestic streaming in Japan, both platforms together drive the majority of the total spent time to watch anime on subscription services.
 As per the data from Media Partners Asia, it states that Prime has over 19 million subscribers in Japan compared to Netflix’s 7.5 million, and it’s mostly because Amazon Prime is bundled cheaply. It also states that anime viewing on Netflix increased from around 3.33 billion hours in the first half of 2023 to around 4.64 billion in the first half of 2026, which shows a great rise.
 × Remove Ads
 The major challenge for a platform like Netflix isn’t just acquiring a big anime catalogue, but understanding the viewing habits of the Japanese. Global streaming success does not automatically dictate domestic dominance in the birthplace of anime.
 Do you think streaming will overtake anime viewing in Japan? Tell us in the comments below.
